This course ideally follows the FSN 408 508 Food Product Development Course as it teaches the final phases of food product development of taking a product into a manufacturing operation and how to ensure optimum performance in production.

title: Principles of Food Packaging
text: Type and application of packaging materials. Migration theories and food package interaction, package testing to ensure safety, and recycling of package materials.

title: Research and Thesis
text: Research and Thesis for Master of Science Degree students.

title: Seminars in FDSN
text: Students attend seminars offered during the semester. Each student is also required to give a 30-minute presentation on a topic of his/her interest or a research project on which she/he has worked.

title: Special Projects
text: Advanced projects in food processing and packaging, food microbiology and safety, food chemistry, and nutrition.

title: Special Problems
text: Independent study of advanced topics in food science and nutrition including food processing and packaging, food microbiology and safety, food chemistry, and nutrition.

title: Continuing of Residence
text: Continuing of residence.

title: Adv Topics Food Microbiology
text: This course is an advanced course in food safety microbiology covering the latest development and trends in food safety related microbiology, including emerging foodborne pathogens of public health significance, as well as the use of the latest technologies for the detection and control of these microbial food safety hazards. This course can be used as credits towards candidature for a Ph.D. degree in Food Safety and Technology/Food Science and Nutrition.

title: Adv Topics Food Chemistry
text: This course can be used as credits towards candidature for a Ph.D. degree in Food Science and Nutrition. This course is expected to cover advanced knowledge in the chemistry of the components of foods, their physiochemical properties and chemical interactions, and the chemical changes that occur during processing, storage, and packaging. Students are expected to work on evidence derived from original research literature, interpretation of research findings, and problem solving based on the scientific principles of food chemistry. This advanced program is open to individuals who hold undergraduate degrees in chemistry, food science, or related disciplines. Students who have completed the FDSN 524 Fundamentals of Food Science and Technology and FDSN 507 Food Analysis courses with a B or higher may also apply. Upon successful completion of this course, students are expected to be able to translate theory and research into practice.

title: Adv Topics Nutrition
text: This course can be used as credits towards candidature for a Ph.D. degree in Food Science and Nutrition. This course is expected to cover advanced knowledge in nutrition, metabolism, disease prevention and health promotion. This advanced program is open to individuals who hold undergraduate degrees in nutritional science, food science, health science, biology, biochemistry, chemistry or related disciplines. Students who have completed the FDSN 501 course with a B or higher may also apply. Upon successful completion of this course, students are expected to be able to translate theory and research into practice.

title: Adv Topics Food Process Engg
text: This course covers recent advancements and developments in food engineering and food processing including novel and emerging processing technologies, advanced thermal process calculations, modeling, simulation, sustainable food processing, process controls & automation and kinetics of food transformations, energy reduction, and food rheology. This course can be used towards candidature for a Ph.D. degree in Food Safety and Technology/Food Science and Nutrition.

title: Research and Thesis
text: Research and Thesis for Ph.D. Food Science Candidates.

title: Research Seminar
text: This course is designed for Ph.D. students to attend research seminars that are presented by invited speakers from academia, food industry and federal government agencies to broaden their understandings and knowledge of various scientific topics and original research in Food Science and Nutrition. This course is mandatory for all Ph.D. students enrolled in the FDSN program. A minimum of 2 credits or 2 semesters of attendance is required for each student. It does not deal with specific techniques per se, but rather with the assumptions and the logic underlying food science and nutrition research. Students will become acquainted with a variety of approaches to research design from the speakers which, in turn, will help to develop their own research projects. A written report that summarizes the major impacts and findings of all presentations is due at the end of the semester.

title: Continuation Gr Studies, Admin
text: This course is open by permit only to graduate students who have non-course and non-thesis requirements to fulfill in the semester of graduation. Permits are entered by Graduate Academic Affairs.

title: GEM ITP
text: This class introduces to game design and experiential media development as professional practice. Students work collaboratively in a studio environment to produce work through iterative design. Additionally, students explore multiple professional specializations within the broader field and develop individual plans for professional development to help guide them towards their academic and professional goals throughout the program.

title: Illness, Care, & Moving Image
text: This course introduces students to how films, video games, and literary texts depict medicine, illness, the human body, and practices of care. Through narrative and documentary media, the course explores how cultural representations shape public understandings of health, suffering, disability, death, and medical authority. Designed for students with no prior background in film studies or medical humanities, the course emphasizes critical viewing, discussion, and reflective analysis.

title: Game Design II
text: Game Design II focuses on professional development cycles and practices as applied to digital game development using a professional development engine. Students work together to form studios and collaborate to complete the development cycle for a single digital game.

title: Worldbuilding for Storytellers
text: This course will take students through the many different aspects of creating an immersive world for storytelling in multiple media, especially fiction writing and game design. Topics covered include, but are not limited to maps, geographic and geopolitical history of a fictional world, environment, ethics and morality, constructed languages, character creation, and backstory.

title: Digital Art
text: Digital Art introduces students to the fundamentals of using modern digital tools creatively. Understanding the tools available is the first step to creative freedom, whether that freedom means being able to make business cards, edit out blemishes from portraits, create digital paintings or making complex memes. The power of software like Photoshop, Illustrator and After Effects becomes available to anyone who has the time it takes to get to know them.

title: Character Art
text: Character Art is a course about the art of crafting, understanding, developing and then embellishing created characters. The course is not solely focused on any one aspect of character related art and design, the course is a robust full-bodied splash-course into all of the related elements of "character" as it applies to fine and commercial art. In this course students will be investigating what makes a successful character for production as well as developing their own characters with the opportunity to work on commercial designs for small indie studios. This course involves writing, acting and image making along with opportunities for collective collaboration between students, faculty & professionals at various levels of industry. Successful, strong, well-developed characters often transcend the stories & mediums they start in, whether traditional or digital, text-based or visual; our aim with this course is an attempt to build successful believable characters that bring the characters, the worlds they inhabit & their stories to life.

title: Philosophy of Games
text: In this course, students will apply philosophical concepts to various dimensions of gaming. Topics will include examining what games are, the ethics of games and gamification, how games can serve as tools for addressing philosophical questions such as identity and agency, and the broader impact of values on individuals and society. Students will challenge their views on games and fundamental philosophical questions through readings, discussions, and activities.

title: Game Design I
text: This course introduces fundamental principles and practices in game design, including game mechanics. During this project-based course, students complete individual and group design projects focused on analog games.

title: Interactive Storytelling
text: Interactive Storytelling examines methods and forms of interactive storytelling in multiple forms. This project-based course provides instruction in narrative techniques while engaging students in the production of original interactive works.

title: Elements of Art
text: Elements of art is a course intended to provide the basic vocabulary of art for both creation and critique AND to develop foundational skills in art for yourself. Art and visual expression has been around as long as we find evidence of human habitation as humans attempt to both capture and record the world and express themselves in it. Students will be drawing a lot. And I mean a lot. Some of these will be quick thumbnail studies that take about a minute each. Some of these will be full compositions that will take multiple hours. We will be engaging in learning communication skills for artists. You will be quizzed on the basic vocabulary, you will write short essays using the terminology of the field, and you will give presentations of your work within the framework of the class. Because it is a humanities class (and because of the nature of art), you will need to talk about art in terms of humanistic expression—what does art have to tell us about who we are as humans? What is included and what is excluded, and why were those decisions made? What, if we dare to ask, is the purpose of individual art pieces or art in general?

Specific topics are listed in the course schedule each semester the class is offered. This course fulfills GEM elective credit for majors and minors and may be repeated for credit when the topic varies.

text: The Game Design and Experiential Media Capstone is a two-semester capstone experience for majors in Game Design. In this two-course sequence, students form studios, conceptualize and develop an original capstone project for an external client.

title: Game Design Capstone II
text: The Game Design and Experiential Media Capstone is a two-semester capstone experience for majors in Game Design. In this two-course sequence, students form studios, conceptualize and develop an original capstone project for an external client.

title: World Civilizations to 1500
text: This course provides an overview of world civilizations from prehistory to 1500, and covers the development of major civilizations in Eurasia, Africa, and the Americas. Topics include: the rise of river civilizations, trade and cultural exchange, the rise of states and empires, and major religious systems to 1500 C.E.

title: World Civilizations Since 1500
text: This course examines the making of the modern world, focusing on the major geopolitical, social, and economic interactions of civilizations around the globe. Topics include: The Age of Colonization and the “Columbian Exchange,” the global impact of the rise of Capitalism and Liberalism, the emergence of Nationalism and Totalitarianism, two world wars, the post-war world and decolonization, and the new geopolitical balance of the new millennium.

title: Western Civilization to 1500
text: A survey of Western Civilization up to 1500. The course covers the rise of cultures and states in Mesopotamia, Greece and Rome, the emergence of important religious systems, medieval Europe, the Crusades, the Black Death, the Renaissance, and the fall of the Eastern Roman Empire in 1453.

title: Western Civ. Since 1500
text: A survey of Western Civilization from 1500. The course covers the Protestant Reformation and the religious wars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment, the French and Industrial Revolutions, the rise of nation states, Nationalism and Imperialism, both world wars, the Cold War, and decolonization.

title: History of the U.S. to 1877
text: This course covers U.S. history up to 1877. Topics covered include the exploration and colonization of North America, colonial society, the American Revolution, the formation of the Constitution, the early years fo the Republic, slavery and the Civil War, and Reconstruction.

title: History of the U.S. Since 1877
text: This class explores how the United States attained economic and military power, and what it did with that power at home and abroad. It covers the Gilded Age, Progressivism, the U.S.’s role in two world wars, the Cold War, the Civil Rights movement, the societal transformation of the 1960s and 1970s, the Reagan and Clinton eras, and the United States in the early years of the new millennium.

title: History of Chicago
text: Basic institutions of the contemporary city studied in their historical context, using Chicago as a case study. Political machines, social and political reform traditions, planning agencies, ethnic neighborhoods, organized crime and many other urban institutions.

title: Prohibition Chicago
text: A study of the people, places, demographics, institutions, politics, culture, and national context of the federal Prohibition (of alcohol) era in Chicago. Students will learn not only about historical events and personages but also consider the interplay of various social, political and economic factors which made the Prohibition era within Chicago unique.

title: Chicago LGBTQ history
text: Development of LGBTQ narratives, cultures and organizations within Chicago with reference to their historical context. Students will learn not only about leaders and significant developments within Chicago LGBTQ history but also learn about local, national, and international developments which aided in formation and development of sexual orientations and gender identities.

title: History of A.I.
text: This course covers the history of artificial intelligence from the mid-20th century up to the present. It explores not only technological developments in the field, but also the philosophy behind the creation and implementation of A.I., as well as its impact on culture, socioeconomics, and the environment today.

title: History of Video Games
text: This course introduces students to the history of video gaming while providing instruction in scholarly practice with an emphasis on research and writing. Topics include the technical and cultural history of the video games, academic writing, and humanities research methods.

Students will apply Humanities perspectives to technical, entrepreneurial, creative, and design projects. They may choose to complete their experience at an organization or business, as a departmental teaching experience, or as an undergraduate research assistantship to a Humanities full-time faculty member. The experience should assist students in professionalization and career decision making. This class is required for all Humanities majors. Students double-majoring in Humanities may fulfill this by submitting a five-page report documenting and demonstrating how an equivalent experience in their other major has fulfilled the learning objectives of this course.

title: Advanced Reading and Writing I
text: Understanding key concepts in design requires proficiency in critical reading of design literature as well as fluid and descriptive written expression. This course will introduce international students to strategies for reading, analyzing, and responding to core texts in the field of design as well as expressing ideas in a variety of writing tasks with clarity and cohesion. Students will engage in critical reading, identify arguments and themes in design-related articles, and convey analysis in written assignments that align with the cultural and academic conventions required in graduate study. Placement in this course is based on exam results and/or departmental approval.

title: Advanced Listen, Presention I
text: Communicating with team members and design professionals requires an advanced level of spoken fluency and proficiency in language. This course will introduce communication strategies necessary for international students to achieve their goals in academic and professional environments. Students will develop increased real-time fluency and clarity in extended discussions of design-related material. The course will also enable students to develop skills in presenting their own designs and design processes. Strategies for effective listening and clear American English pronunciation will also be covered.

title: Advanced Reading & Writing II
text: This course will build on previously learned skills to teach international students language related to the professional practice of design. Students will learn to read design-related texts more critically by uncovering a writer's assumptions and evaluating an article's validity. Students will also develop different aspects of writing for design, including research and synthesis in response and essay writing, among others. Placement in this course is based on exam results and/or successful completion of IDN 461 Advanced Reading and Writing for Design I

title: Advanced Listen, Present II
text: This course will teach advanced communication strategies necessary for design students to interact in academic and professional contexts. Students will develop their critical listening and discussion skills with extended discourse on design topics. Students will also develop greater fluency, accuracy, and clarity through a semester-length project. This course will enable students to build confidence in presentation, discussion, and project work. Placement in this course is based on placement exam results and/or the successful completion of IDN 462 Advanced listening and Presentation in Design I

Includes a culminating project that demonstrates basic principles of screen design and computer-human interaction using a variety of media. Projects require use of common software applications for creating and editing six data types -- text, bitmap, geometry, sound, animation, and video.

title: Survey Methods

Students will learn how to design, understand, and evaluate surveys and other quantitative research tools and techniques as well as how to use online survey tools in their own work.

This exploration will happen across the four critical elements of a new venture: brand / value proposition; user experience; business model; and organization. Students will walk away with an understanding of how to architect new ventures using a combination of user empathy, market data, and intuition.

Students may take this class multiple times, non-concurrently, for a maximum of 12 credits towards their degree.
